title: Pink-sand coves and mountain villages of western Crete
shortDescription: 8 nights between the old Venetian harbour of Chania and the lagoons of Balos and Elafonissi.
description:
Western Crete is the bit of Greece people whisper about when they don't want the cruise ships to find it. The light is softer than Santorini, the food is heavier and better, and the mountains drop straight into the sea without bothering to fade out first.

You stay in a restored Venetian townhouse in the old harbour of Chania — stone walls, blue shutters, a roof terrace that looks straight at the lighthouse. From there we run day trips by boat to Balos lagoon, by 4x4 down the Samaria gorge, and inland to villages where the kafenio serves raki at ten in the morning and nobody finds that strange.

The tour is paced for slow travel. Two long lunches in mountain tavernas, a sunset swim at Elafonissi when the day-trippers leave, an afternoon learning to make bougatsa from the family who has been doing it on Skrydlof street since 1924. You'll come back tanned, slightly heavier, and convinced you've seen the real Greece.

Private boat day to Balos lagoon, before the crowds
Samaria gorge descent with a local guide
Bougatsa workshop with the Iordanis family
Sunset swim at Elafonissi's pink sand

title: Espresso, ruins and rooftop suppers in the eternal city
shortDescription: 5 nights in a Trastevere palazzo with a private guide to the parts of Rome the guidebooks miss.
description:
Most people see Rome in a hurry — three days, queue for the Colosseum, queue for the Vatican, leave with sore feet and a memory of crowds. We do it differently. Five nights gives you time to live there, not just visit.

You stay in a converted 17th-century palazzo in Trastevere, the neighbourhood where Romans actually live and eat. The owner Federica brings up cornetti in the morning and knows which trattoria has the best amatriciana on any given Tuesday. From your front door it's a ten-minute walk across the river to the Forum.

The sightseeing is real but the pace is human. Vatican Museums on a private after-hours tour when the crowds are gone. A dawn walk through the Forum with an archaeologist. A pasta workshop in a Roman grandmother's kitchen. And a long evening on a friend's rooftop with a view of the dome of Saint Peter's, eating cacio e pepe and arguing about which gelato is best.

title: Glaciers, geysers and the green sky of the north
shortDescription: 7 nights chasing waterfalls, ice caves and the aurora around Iceland's Ring Road.
description:
Iceland in winter is the closest most of us will get to another planet. Black sand, blue ice, sulphur steam rising out of the ground, and on a clear night a slow green ribbon dancing across the entire sky.

We give you the south coast and the highlands by 4x4 with a driver-guide who grew up here and reads the weather like a book. You sleep in remote farm hotels with hot tubs facing the dark, and a wake-up call when the aurora forecast spikes. No buses, no crowds, no fixed itinerary on aurora nights — we chase the cloud gaps wherever they are.

The daytime is just as good. A guided walk inside a crystal-blue glacier ice cave. The waterfalls of Seljalandsfoss and Skógafoss from behind the curtain. A long soak in a wild hot spring on the way home. And on the last evening, the Blue Lagoon, properly, with a glass of champagne in the steam.

title: Gaudí mornings and vermouth afternoons
shortDescription: 4 nights in the Born district with private access to Sagrada Família and a tapas crawl with a local chef.
description:
Barcelona rewards people who slow down. The Sagrada Família is overwhelming when you're herded through it in a tour group of fifty, but quietly devastating when you sit on a bench inside at opening time with the light coming through Gaudí's coloured glass.

We put you in a converted modernist apartment in the Born district, two minutes from the Picasso museum and ten from the beach. The mornings are for monuments — private early access to the Sagrada, a long walk through Park Güell before the cruise crowds, a slow lunch at the Boqueria market. The afternoons are for what Catalans actually do: vermouth at noon, a swim, a siesta, dinner at ten.

A local chef takes you on a proper tapas crawl through five neighbourhood bars in Gràcia — anchovies in vermouth, bombas, patatas bravas, and the kind of bocadillo you can't get in a tourist trap. You'll leave understanding why this city has more Michelin stars per capita than almost anywhere on earth.

shortDescription: 4 nights in Mala Strana, a private castle tour after closing, and a beer cellar crawl with a brewer.
description:
Prague has the rare gift of being beautiful from absolutely every angle. The red rooftops from the castle hill, the river bridges in the morning mist, the baroque squares with their astronomical clocks — and somehow despite the Instagram crowds it still feels like a city that belongs to itself.

We put you in a small hotel under the castle in Mala Strana, the quieter side of the river, ten minutes from the Charles Bridge but a world away from the tour groups. Mornings are for walking — across the bridge before sunrise, up the old castle stairs when the cobblestones are still wet.

The Czech beer story is older and more interesting than the German one, and a Prague brewer takes you on a cellar crawl through five micro-breweries you won't find in the guidebooks. Sausage, dumplings, dark lager, the proper kind. End the trip with a chamber concert in a baroque palace built into the hillside.

title: Bamboo, tea bowls and a thousand red gates
shortDescription: 7 nights in a ryokan in Higashiyama with a Zen monk, a tea master and a private kaiseki dinner.
description:
Kyoto is a city that asks you to slow down. The temples are open at five in the morning, the tea ceremonies take an hour for what could be done in two minutes, and even the most ordinary lunch arrives on six lacquered dishes arranged with the care of a small landscape.

We stay you in a family-run ryokan in Higashiyama, the old eastern hills — futons on tatami, a deep wooden bath that smells of cypress, breakfast that arrives in seventeen small bowls. From the front door you can walk to Kiyomizu temple before the gates open and have the whole hillside to yourself.

The week mixes the famous and the quiet. Fushimi Inari's thousand red gates at dawn. A morning of zazen meditation with a Zen monk at Daitoku-ji. A proper tea ceremony with a master who learned from her grandfather. A long evening in a kaiseki restaurant where the chef has been refining one menu for forty years. And one day of nothing — just the bamboo grove of Arashiyama and a long lunch by the river.

shortDescription: 9 nights split between an Ubud jungle villa and an over-water bungalow off Nusa Lembongan.
description:
Bali still has both sides of itself, if you know where to go. The serious Hindu island of temples and offerings, and the relaxed island of surf breaks and reef snorkels. We give you both.

Four nights in a villa with its own pool overlooking the rice terraces above Ubud — silver monkeys in the trees, the gamelan from the next village in the evening, a private chef who cooks dinner on your terrace. From there we do the temples, the Tegallalang terraces, a morning of yoga with a Balinese teacher, and a day in a wood-carving workshop.

Then the boat south to Nusa Lembongan, an island a tenth the size of Bali. Five nights in an over-water bungalow with a glass floor and the reef right under your feet. Manta ray snorkel at Manta Point, sunset SUP across Mangrove Bay, and absolutely nothing scheduled for the last two days except sleep, sea and books.

shortDescription: 6 nights in a luxury over-water villa in Baa Atoll's UNESCO biosphere with daily reef excursions.

The Maldives is one of those places where the brochure photos turn out to be honest. The water really is that colour. The reef really does start two metres from the deck. The manta rays really do pass under the glass floor at five in the afternoon during plankton season.

We place you in Baa Atoll, the UNESCO biosphere reserve, in a one-bedroom over-water villa with a private plunge pool, sun deck and direct ladder access to the reef. The resort is small, low-key, more honeymooners and ocean-obsessed couples than influencer chaos. House-reef snorkelling is unlimited and genuinely world-class.

The package is mostly about doing nothing very well — breakfast brought to the deck on a tray, an afternoon at the over-water spa, a private sandbank picnic at sunset. But for the two of you who want a little adventure, we add a guided snorkel at Hanifaru Bay during manta season, a sunset dolphin cruise and a stargazing dinner on an uninhabited island.

title: The Inca trail to the cloud city
shortDescription: 9 nights from Cusco through the Sacred Valley with a private guide and sunrise at Machu Picchu.
description:
Machu Picchu deserves more than a day trip from Cusco. The site is at its best in the slow hour after sunrise when the buses haven't arrived and the clouds are still moving through the ruins, and it's at its quietest if you stay overnight in the village below and walk up before dawn.

We build the trip around acclimatisation. Three nights in the Sacred Valley first — lower altitude than Cusco, soft mornings in a colonial hacienda, salt pans of Maras and the circular terraces of Moray with a private archaeologist. Then the Vistadome train to Aguas Calientes and a full day at Machu Picchu with sunrise access.

From there we hand you back to the highlands. Cusco proper for three nights — the cathedral, the Coricancha sun temple, a long lunch at Central, time for the textile women of Chinchero. We finish with a slow flight to Lima for a final night and a long ceviche dinner at one of the world's best restaurants.

title: Harbour swims, opera nights and the bluest mountains

Sydney is a city that takes itself less seriously than it should. title: Cliff-edge villages and lemon-grove lunches
shortDescription: 7 nights in a Positano cliff hotel with a private boat day to Capri and a long lunch in Ravello.
description:
The Amalfi coast is one of those places that's been famous for so long it could easily have been ruined. It hasn't. Seven nights in a cliffside hotel above Positano — every room with a sea balcony, breakfast on a terrace that drops straight to the water, a path down to a small beach club where the loungers are blue-and-white striped and the spritz arrives without you asking. A private boat day around Capri's Faraglioni, into the Blue Grotto if the tide allows, lunch at La Fontelina on the rocks.

A long lunch at Ravello's Villa Cimbrone with the infinity view, a lemon-grove tour with a family who has been pressing limoncello for four generations, a sunset on the Path of the Gods cliff walk. And on the last evening, a fishing-boat dinner of whatever came in that day, eaten with your feet in the sand on the Amalfi beach.

Sicily is its own country, with its own language, its own light and its own food. Nine nights gives you time to see the three Sicilies that don't really know each other — the elegant Greek east, the baroque south, and the gloriously chaotic Arabic-Norman west.

Three nights in Taormina, the cliff-edge resort town the Romans loved and the British inherited. A clifftop hotel with a sea pool, a morning at the Greek theatre with Etna smoking behind, a swim at Isola Bella below. A jeep climb to the summit craters of Etna with a vulcanologist.

Three nights in Noto — the most beautiful baroque town you've never heard of, where the buildings are made of soft yellow stone that glows pink at sunset. Long lunches in Modica with the chocolate that's still made the way the Aztecs made it. Then three nights in Palermo — the chaotic, dirty, brilliant capital where the best meal of your trip will probably be a panelle sandwich eaten standing up at the Vucciria market.

title: Bistros, bookshops and a private hour at the Louvre
shortDescription: 5 nights in a Marais apartment with a Louvre after-hours tour and a long Sunday at the markets.
description:
Paris doesn't reveal itself to people in a hurry. The five-night version we run is built around walking, eating slowly, and the time of day when the light goes copper on the Haussmann facades — about 7 pm in summer, 5 pm in winter, and worth being outside for.

We put you in a small apartment in the Marais, on a quiet pedestrian street between Place des Vosges and the river. Mornings are for the things you have to see done properly — a private after-hours hour in the Louvre with an Egyptologist (you stand in front of Liberty with about six other people instead of six hundred), a slow morning at Musée d'Orsay before the lines.

The rest is what makes Paris Paris. A Sunday morning at the Bastille market followed by long lunch in the apartment with what you bought. A perfume class with a working nose in the 8th. A bouquiniste book browse along the Seine. And an evening dinner at a tiny bistro on rue Paul Bert where the menu is on a chalkboard and the bread is still warm.

title: Lavender fields, rosé afternoons and village markets
shortDescription: 7 nights in a Luberon mas with a chef cooking class and a private boat day to the Calanques.
description:
The Provençal cliché is real and it is wonderful. Yes, the lavender does turn the hills purple in July. Yes, the rosé is best at lunchtime with a bowl of olives. Yes, every village really does have a Saturday market that hasn't changed in two hundred years. We just give you the version with no tour buses.

Seven nights in a restored 18th-century stone farmhouse outside Lourmarin, in the heart of the Luberon. Olive trees, lavender at the door in season, a pool that looks at the Ventoux mountain. Marie the housekeeper brings warm croissants every morning and tells you what's happening in which village that day.

The week is structured around markets — Tuesday Gordes, Friday Lourmarin, Saturday Apt — and slow lunches under plane trees. We add a sunrise hot-air balloon over the Sénanque abbey lavender, a half-day cooking class with chef Anne in her kitchen, a Châteauneuf-du-Pape tasting day, and a private boat from Cassis along the Calanques cliffs. The pace is intentionally slow.

title: Belle époque promenades and turquoise corniches
shortDescription: 5 nights in a Nice belle-époque hotel with a private corniche drive to Èze and a long lunch in Saint-Paul-de-Vence.
description:
The French Riviera is one of those places where the cliché came from the place, not the other way around. The light really is that golden. The sea really is that turquoise. The little stone villages on the corniche really do look like a Cézanne, because Cézanne lived here.

We put you in a small belle-époque hotel on a quiet street in Nice — five minutes from the Promenade des Anglais but tucked away from the noise. Mornings on the pebble beach with the loungers and the rosé, afternoons in the old town for a socca and a granita, evenings in the harbour district for the freshest fish in town.

A private car-and-driver takes you along the Moyenne Corniche to Èze for a sunrise on the medieval village clinging to a cliff over the sea, then on to Monaco for a slow lunch at the Café de Paris. A separate day inland to Saint-Paul-de-Vence — Chagall's grave, the Fondation Maeght, and a long lunch at La Colombe d'Or where the Picassos and Matisses on the walls came as payment for meals.

description:
Lisbon has the rare quality of being beautiful without trying to be. The city tumbles down seven hills to the Tagus, painted with blue azulejo tiles and faded pastel facades, and the yellow trams clatter up streets too steep for cars. Five nights is enough to feel like you live there.

We put you in a converted apartment in Alfama, the old Moorish quarter that survived the 1755 earthquake. From your window you can see the Tagus and hear the fado from the bars below at night. Mornings for the famous viewpoints — Senhora do Monte, Santa Catarina — and afternoons for slow lunches at tascas where everyone is a regular.

A tile-painting workshop with a third-generation azulejo painter teaches you the technique that has covered Portugal's walls for five hundred years. A fado evening in a tiny Alfama bar where the singer is also the cook. And a day trip to Sintra — Pena palace in the morning light, lunch in the village, the cliffs of Cabo da Roca at the edge of Europe.

title: Port lodges, river boats and a Douro vineyard
shortDescription: 6 nights between Porto's old town and a quinta in the Douro valley with a river-boat day.
description:
Porto is the kind of city that feels older than it is, mostly because the river running through it is timeless. The port-wine lodges still line the Gaia bank, the rabelo boats still come down from the Douro vineyards in the autumn, and the old men still gather in the market every morning to argue about football.

Three nights in Porto in a small hotel above the Ribeira riverside — the Dom Luís bridge two minutes away, the lodges of Taylor's, Graham's and Sandeman across the water. A vintage tasting at a working port lodge, a long lunch at a tasca where the petisco menu changes daily, and a Saturday morning at the Bolhão market.

Then three nights at a wine quinta in the Douro valley — terraced vineyards rolling down to the river, breakfast on a stone terrace, a small pool that looks at a view that hasn't changed in three hundred years. A river-boat day from Pinhão through the schist gorges, lunch on board, vineyard walks with the cellarmaster. The drive back to Porto on the last morning is a slow one.

title: Levada walks and Atlantic cliffs of the floating garden
shortDescription: 7 nights in a Funchal cliff hotel with daily levada walks and a sunrise on Pico do Arieiro.
description:
Madeira is what Hawaii would be like if it had been settled by 15th-century Portuguese instead of 18th-century American whalers. A volcanic Atlantic island covered in laurel forest, with a thousand kilometres of irrigation channels — the levadas — running along the cliffs and through the woods. You walk along them all week.

Seven nights in a small hotel on the cliff edge above Funchal, looking south at the open ocean and east at the lights of the old town. Mornings on different levada walks — Caldeirão Verde through the tunnels and waterfalls, the 25 fontes with its laurel canopy, the easy Levada do Rei. A guide for two days, on your own for the easy ones with a printed map.

The non-walking half is just as good. A sunrise on Pico do Arieiro above the clouds. A wine tasting at the Blandy's lodge in old Funchal. A market morning at the Mercado dos Lavradores for tropical fruit you've never seen. A toboggan ride down the Monte cobblestones in a wicker basket pushed by men in straw hats, an experience that should not work but somehow does.

title: Lochs, lonely glens and the Cuillin ridge
shortDescription: 7 nights driving the Highlands and Skye with a private guide and a whisky tasting on Islay.
description:
The Scottish Highlands are big in a way that surprises people from anywhere flatter. Empty glens that take an hour to drive through, a single road across the Skye Cuillins, lochs so still on a good morning that the mountains read upside-down in the water. You need a car, a week, and a thermos.

We build the trip around the long views. Three nights in a converted Victorian lodge by Loch Ness — fireplace, library, breakfast looking at the loch. From there we run day trips up Glen Affric and out to Cawdor castle, and a long single-track drive through Glen Coe.

Then three nights on Skye in a small inn above Portree harbour — the Cuillin ridge in every window, the Old Man of Storr a twenty-minute drive, a sunset at the Quiraing that no photograph has ever done justice to. And we finish with one night on Islay for a whisky tasting at Lagavulin and Ardbeg, picked up by a small plane from Glasgow on the way back. It's a long, slow, beautiful week.

title: Red fishermen's cabins and the green sky above Lofoten
shortDescription: 7 nights in a Lofoten rorbu cabin with aurora chasing and a winter fjord cruise.
description:
Lofoten in winter is one of those places that ruins other landscapes for you. Granite peaks rise straight out of the dark sea, red fishermen's cabins cluster on the small flats between, and on a clear night the aurora dances above the mountain ridge like it's putting on a show for you specifically.

We put you in a traditional rorbu — a fisherman's cabin on stilts over the water — in the village of Reine, the most photographed place in northern Norway for reasons you'll understand immediately. Wood-burning stove, sauna, a window onto the fjord. You can walk straight out the front door and onto a kayak in the morning.

The week mixes still days and big ones. A winter fjord cruise to the dramatic Trollfjord. A guided photo workshop on the aurora with a local night-sky photographer. A snowshoe walk to a frozen viewpoint above the Reine bay. And one slow day where the only plan is the sauna, the sea swim, and a book. The last evening we go to Henningsvær for a final dinner at a 200-year-old quayside restaurant.

title: Old city walls and an Adriatic island day
shortDescription: 6 nights in a Dubrovnik old-town apartment with a private Elaphiti islands cruise and a Korčula day.
description:
Dubrovnik can feel overrun in high season — the cruise ships, the Game of Thrones tours, the people in front of you on the city walls. Done in the shoulder season with a few right decisions, it's still one of the great walled cities of the Mediterranean.

We put you in a small stone apartment inside the walls, on a quiet alley below the Jesuit church. The trick is to be inside the walls when the day-trippers leave at 6 pm — the limestone streets are empty, the warm stone glows, and the city becomes the medieval republic it was for four hundred years.

The daytime is on the water. A private cruise through the three Elaphiti islands — Koločep, Lopud, Šipan — anchored swims, lunch on board, an empty beach on Lopud. A long day trip to Korčula, an hour's catamaran north — the supposed birthplace of Marco Polo, with a tiny walled centre half the size of Dubrovnik and a tenth the crowds. And a slow walk along the city walls at opening time, before the heat. The cable car up Mount Srđ at sunset on the last evening.

shortDescription: 7 nights between Split's old town inside a Roman palace and the island of Hvar.
description:

Last night at the harbourside in Hvar town watching the boats come in.

title: The Matterhorn from every angle and a glacier express
shortDescription: 6 nights in car-free Zermatt with the Glacier Express train, Gornergrat sunrise and a glacier hike.
description:
Zermatt is one of the few places where the cliché is actually that good. The Matterhorn is the most photographed mountain in the world, and the reason is that no matter how many photos you've seen, the first time you walk out of the train station and see it standing there impossibly above the village, it stops you for a second.

We put you in a small wooden chalet hotel a few minutes from the centre, with a balcony that has the Matterhorn in it. Zermatt has been car-free since the 1960s — the only traffic is the electric carts and the horse-drawn sleighs in winter — and you can walk anywhere in fifteen minutes.

The week is built around the train and the mountain. A sunrise on Gornergrat (the train up at dawn, croissants in the summit hotel as the light hits the peak). A glacier hike on the Theodul. A spa afternoon at the Riffelalp at 2200m. A long day on the Glacier Express train through to St Moritz and back. And, the unmissable thing, a sunset dinner at one of the high-altitude mountain restaurants where the gondola takes you back down in the dark.

title: Coffee houses, the Belvedere and a night at the opera
shortDescription: 4 nights in a Ringstrasse townhouse with a Belvedere private hour and a Vienna State Opera evening.

Vienna is a city where the coffee house is still a kind of public living room and the line for the standing tickets at the State Opera starts at 4 pm for an 8 pm performance. It moves at a 19th-century pace and is deliberately better for it.

Mornings of long breakfasts in proper coffee houses — Café Central, Café Sperl, Café Hawelka — with the marble tables and the surly waiters in tailcoats who have been there for thirty years.

The culture is what you came for. A private opening hour at the Belvedere palace with Klimt's Kiss before the doors open. A standing-room ticket at the State Opera so you can see how Vienna actually does it. A walk through the Hofburg and the Spanish Riding School, with the Lipizzaners doing their morning training. And on the last evening, a Sachertorte at the Sacher hotel and a long carriage ride through the old town as the Christmas lights come on (or the plane trees turn, depending on the season).

title: An island church on a glacial lake and the turquoise Soča river
shortDescription: 6 nights split Lake Bled and the Soča valley with a private pletna boat and a rafting morning.
description:
Slovenia is the small alpine country that quietly does most things better than its more famous neighbours. The food is better than you'd expect, the wine is shockingly good, the lakes are postcard-perfect and there are roughly ten people in front of you in any queue.

Three nights at Lake Bled in a small hotel above the lake — every room with a balcony looking at the island church and the cliff castle. Mornings for a pletna boat (the traditional gondola-rowed boats with the wedding cake island) to the church on the island, where you ring the bell for a wish. Afternoons walking the lake (six kilometres flat) or up to the Mala Osojnica viewpoint for the picture-postcard angle.

Then three nights west into the Soča valley, where the Julian Alps drop into the most surreally turquoise river you'll ever see. A small lodge in Kobarid, where Hemingway set Farewell to Arms. A rafting morning on the Soča (gentle in summer, rocky in spring), a walk to the Kozjak waterfall, a long lunch at Hiša Franko, a two-Michelin-star Slovenian restaurant that's also one of the warmest. And one rest day where the only plan is the riverside terrace and a book.

title: Thermal baths, ruin bars and a Danube boat at dusk
shortDescription: 4 nights between Buda and Pest with the Széchenyi baths, ruin-bar crawl and a chamber concert on the Danube.
description:
Budapest is the most beautiful city in central Europe that nobody outside central Europe properly knows. The river splits it in two — Buda on the hills, Pest on the flats — and the Hungarian parliament across the water at night looks like an opera set someone forgot to take down.

We put you in a small hotel on the Pest side, two minutes from the river and ten from the opera. Mornings for the museums and the market hall, afternoons for the baths. Hungary has a different relationship with thermal water than the rest of Europe — there are seven public baths inside the city, all running, all heated by the underground hot springs, all genuinely social spaces rather than spas. Széchenyi in the Városliget park is the largest and the most theatrical.

The evenings get loose. A ruin-bar crawl with a Pest local through five Jewish-quarter bars that occupy abandoned tenement buildings — fairy lights, mismatched furniture, the best pálinka in the country. A chamber concert on a Danube boat at dusk, with the parliament lit up and the bridges starting to twinkle. And on the last night, a goulash dinner at a Buda old-town tavern and a slow walk back over the chain bridge.

shortDescription: 8 nights between a Phuket beach hotel and the Phi Phi islands with a private longtail day.
description:
Phuket gets a bad press for being overdeveloped, and parts of it are. The trick is to stay on the less obvious west coast beaches and to use the island as a base for the much better day-trips out to the Andaman archipelago.

Five nights at a beach hotel on Surin or Kamala — the quieter, prettier north-west coast, where the sunsets are over the Andaman and the beach is still mostly empty before 10 am. Long mornings on the sand, afternoons of Thai massage and a swim, evenings at the night markets of Patong (a 30-minute taxi) or a fine-dining dinner at Pru in the jungle.

The big day is a private longtail to the Phi Phi islands — Maya Bay (where they filmed The Beach), the snorkel at Bamboo Island, lunch on board. Then we move you for three nights to a small island resort on Koh Yao Noi in the middle of Phang Nga Bay — limestone cliffs straight out of a James Bond film, empty beaches, no roads. Kayak through the sea caves, watch the longtails come in at dusk, eat seafood that was swimming this morning.

title: Walled old town, ethical elephants and a jungle waterfall
shortDescription: 6 nights in a Chiang Mai old-town guesthouse with an ethical elephant sanctuary and a hill-tribe stay.
description:
Chiang Mai is the spiritual home of the Lanna kingdom and the unofficial backpacker capital of southeast Asia, but stripped of the backpacker reputation it's actually one of the best slow-travel cities in the world. The old town is small, walled, full of 14th-century temples, and the food is famous for a reason — northern Thai cuisine is its own thing.

Four nights in a small teak-and-stone guesthouse inside the old town walls — a courtyard pool, breakfast under the bodhi tree, ten minutes' walk to Wat Phra Singh. A morning at the temples, an afternoon at the Saturday walking street, a sunset at Doi Suthep above the city.

The big experience is the elephant day — at a proper, ethical sanctuary 90 minutes outside the city where the elephants have been rescued from the logging industry and you feed and walk with them but you do not ride them. A morning of bathing in the river and a long lunch at the sanctuary. Then two nights in a hill-tribe village two hours north — a homestay in a Karen long-house, jungle walks, a working-elephant retirement project, and a swim in a waterfall on the way back to Chiang Mai. Last evening cooking class with the Thai grandmother who runs the guesthouse kitchen.

title: Old quarter pho, water puppets and a junk in Halong
shortDescription: 7 nights between Hanoi's old quarter and a luxury junk in Halong Bay with a Sapa rice-terrace night.
description:
Vietnam is one of those countries where one week is genuinely enough to see something proper. The north has Hanoi, Halong Bay and the mountains of Sapa stacked close together, and the contrasts between them — frenetic capital, silent islands, terraced rice fields in cloud — are part of why you go.

Three nights in a small boutique hotel in Hanoi's old quarter. Mornings at the temple of literature and the Hoan Kiem lake, afternoons of the museums, evenings of pho on a tiny street-side plastic stool and a Bia Hoi (fresh draft beer, less than a dollar) on the corner of Ta Hien street. A water-puppet show at the Thang Long theatre, an evening street-food walking tour with a Hanoi local.

Then two nights on a luxury junk in Halong Bay. Forty-cabin junk, private balcony, kayaks from the lower deck, anchored every evening in a cove between the limestone karsts. Tai chi at dawn on the upper deck, cooking class on board, swim from a tiny private beach. Then back to land and a sleeper train north to Sapa for one night in a hill-tribe lodge with the rice terraces in every direction. A long final dinner in Hanoi.

title: Lantern-lit nights and a Mekong delta morning
shortDescription: 6 nights between Hoi An's old town, the My Son temples and a Mekong river homestay.
description:
Hoi An is the small old trading town in central Vietnam that the war didn't reach. The riverfront is lined with 17th-century merchants' houses, the streets are still narrow enough to require bicycles, and every evening the lanterns above the river light up and the city becomes a different colour.

Four nights in a small boutique hotel five minutes' walk from the old town, by a paddy field. A pool, breakfast on a courtyard, bicycles. Mornings at the museums and the Japanese covered bridge, afternoons at a tailor (Hoi An is famous for them — you can have a properly made suit or a silk dress finished in 24 hours), evenings on the river with a lantern-paper boat sent down the current.

The two day-trips are the My Son Hindu temple complex — Cham kingdom ruins from the 4th century, a slow morning with no crowds and a knowing guide — and a long day on the Mekong delta further south. Sampans through the floating markets, a homestay overnight at Ben Tre with a Vietnamese family, breakfast with the river fishermen, and a long boat back through coconut and rice fields. A cooking class on the last day with a chef who teaches you four central-Vietnamese classics.

title: Pink-sand beaches, manta rays and the dragons of Komodo
shortDescription: 7 nights on a private liveaboard schooner around Komodo with manta dives and dragon walks.
description:
Komodo is the kind of place that doesn't get enough credit because it's a five-hour flight from Bali to get there. The reward is one of the last reef-and-island wildernesses in southeast Asia — pink-sand beaches, manta-ray cleaning stations the size of football pitches, and prehistoric dragons that hunt water buffalo on dry land.

We put you on a small private wooden phinisi schooner — the traditional Indonesian sailing vessel, four cabins, captain, chef, dive master. You sleep on board for six nights and never see another tour group on the islands. Sunrises from the deck, sunsets in a different cove every day, and seafood that an hour earlier was swimming next to the boat.

The itinerary is built around the wildlife and the snorkel. A guided ranger walk on Komodo island and Rinca to see the dragons (the rangers carry forked sticks — the dragons do bite). Two dives or snorkels at Manta Point, where a dozen mantas at once is normal. Hidden beaches at Padar with the famous three-bay viewpoint. Pink Beach for the sand that's actually pink. A village stop at Mesa island where the kids run out to the boat. One last night in a hotel above Labuan Bajo to decompress.

title: Volcano sunrise, the largest Buddhist monument and a batik workshop
shortDescription: 6 nights in Yogyakarta with a Borobudur dawn, a Prambanan sunset and a Mount Merapi jeep day.
description:
Java is the most populous island in the world, and Yogyakarta is its cultural heart — the city of sultans, batik, gamelan, and the largest Buddhist monument on earth fifteen minutes' drive away. It rewards the slow traveller in a way Bali doesn't.

Six nights in a heritage hotel in the Prawirotaman district, near the kraton (the sultan's palace) and the small batik workshops of Tirto Diningratan. Mornings of cycle rickshaws (becaks) through the old town, afternoons of long lunches at a Javanese rumah makan, evenings of gamelan rehearsals in the open pendopo halls.

The big mornings are the temples. Borobudur at dawn — a private climb up the nine terraces of the world's largest Buddhist monument with the mist still rising from the rainforest, six hours before the tour buses. Prambanan, the Hindu compound across the plain, at sunset. A Mount Merapi jeep day on the still-smoking active volcano with a guide who survived the 2010 eruption. A batik workshop where you draw your own design with wax and dye it twice in indigo. Last night a Ramayana ballet performed against the lit-up Prambanan towers.

title: Pink, blue and golden cities of the Maharajas
shortDescription: 9 nights through the Rajasthan classics — Jaipur, Jodhpur, Jaisalmer and Udaipur — in heritage palace hotels.
description:
Rajasthan is the kind of trip that ruins other trips. Nine nights moving between former maharaja palaces converted into hotels, with private cars between, a guide who's a historian, and the kind of stories that involve real tigers and real elephants and the time a peacock attacked the royal cook.

We start in Jaipur — the pink city. Three nights at the Samode Haveli in the old town. The Amer fort on an elephant in the morning, the City Palace and Hawa Mahal in the afternoon, the bangle bazaar at sunset. A long drive west to Jodhpur — the blue city under the Mehrangarh fort. Two nights at a city palace overlooking the indigo rooftops. Then on to Jaisalmer in the Thar desert — the golden city, made of yellow sandstone that glows at dusk. Two nights at Suryagarh, a fort-style hotel outside town. A camel ride at sunset to a dune camp for dinner under more stars than you've ever seen.

The trip finishes in Udaipur — the white city, on a lake. Two nights at the Taj Lake Palace, the white marble hotel that sits on its own island. A boat across the water at sunset, a long sufi-music dinner at the palace, and one slow day where the only plan is the room balcony, the lake and a book.

title: Houseboat backwaters, tea hills and an ayurvedic week
shortDescription: 8 nights through Kerala — Kochi, Munnar tea hills, a houseboat on the backwaters and a beach finale at Marari.
description:
Kerala is the un-stressful India. The southern state where the food is gentler, the air is wetter, the politics are quietly communist, and the literacy rate is closer to Sweden's than to Mumbai's. Eight nights here is a slow week even by slow-travel standards.

Two nights in Kochi — Portuguese Fort Kochi neighbourhood, Chinese fishing nets on the waterfront, a Jewish quarter from the 16th century. A long afternoon of cardamom and turmeric at the spice market.

Then up to Munnar in the tea hills — three thousand metres of altitude and a thousand square kilometres of tea estates. Two nights at a colonial-era bungalow above a tea plantation, walks through the bushes with a tea master, a long lunch in the cardamom forest.

Down to the backwaters for two nights on a traditional kettuvallam houseboat — a teak-and-coir vessel with a private bedroom, a kitchen on board, and a slow drift through the canals, paddy fields and Christian villages of the Alappuzha delta. Last two nights at Marari beach, in a thatched-roof villa five steps from the sand, with a daily ayurvedic massage and absolutely nothing scheduled.

title: Tea trains, leopard safaris and a south-coast beach finale
shortDescription: 9 nights across Sri Lanka — cultural triangle, hill country tea train and the south coast.
description:
Sri Lanka is the most concentrated trip in Asia. Two thousand years of Buddhist history, a UNESCO triangle of ancient capitals, the most beautiful train journey in the world through the tea hills, and a south coast with leopards in the morning and turtles in the evening. Nine nights does it all properly.

We start at Sigiriya — the lion rock, a 5th-century palace on top of a 200-metre rock pinnacle, painted with frescoes that have survived the rain. Two nights at a jungle lodge below the rock, a sunrise climb up the staircase, and a half-day at Polonnaruwa with the ancient stone Buddhas. Then a day in Kandy with the temple of the tooth and a tea-museum night above the city.

Then the train. Kandy to Ella, six hours through the highest tea hills in the country — the locals hang out of the open doors, the train slows for the viaducts, the conductor sells you a tea and a samosa. Two nights at a colonial tea bungalow above Ella with the morning mist in the valley. Then south to Yala for a leopard safari at dawn and dusk for one night, and four nights at a quiet beach hotel at Tangalle — long walks at low tide, turtle hatchlings released at dusk, slow last dinners on the sand.

title: Jungle temples and the dawn at Angkor
shortDescription: 5 nights in Siem Reap with a 3-day Angkor pass, a Tonle Sap stilt-village boat and a temple-restoration visit.
description:
Angkor Wat is the most famous of the temples, but the whole Angkor complex is a city of stone the size of modern Paris, with two hundred ruined temples scattered through the jungle. Three days to do it properly with a guide is the right number.

Five nights at a small French-colonial hotel in the old French quarter of Siem Reap. Pool, breakfast on a courtyard, ten minutes' tuk-tuk to the temple complex. Tuk-tuks all week with a driver who knows the routes through the jungle to skip the buses.

Day one is the famous one — Angkor Wat at sunrise (the standard photo, with the towers reflected in the pond, which is genuinely worth being there for), then the small temples of the east. Day two is the big circuit — Ta Prohm where the strangler figs eat the stones (the Lara Croft temple), the bas-reliefs of the Bayon at the centre of Angkor Thom. Day three is the further temples — Banteay Srei with the pink sandstone, Beng Mealea swallowed by jungle. Plus an afternoon at the artisan workshop where they're restoring a temple piece by piece. And a Tonle Sap boat day to the stilt villages above the lake.

title: Saffron-robed mornings on the Mekong
shortDescription: 5 nights in a French-colonial Luang Prabang guesthouse with the dawn alms ceremony and a slow boat upstream.
description:
Luang Prabang is one of those places that's somehow held onto exactly the version of itself that the brochure photos sell. UNESCO has helped — no buildings above two storeys, no traffic in the old town between four and six pm, and the saffron-robed monks of the thirty Theravada temples in the centre still walk the dawn alms route the way they have for six hundred years.

Five nights in a French-colonial guesthouse on the peninsula between the Mekong and the Khan. Twelve rooms, a courtyard pool, a teak veranda for breakfast looking at the river. Mornings of slow walks along the riverside, afternoons of the museums in the old palace, evenings at the night market for the textile-and-silver crafts and an Aperol on the river.

The two must-dos are the alms ceremony — 5:30 am, in respectful silence, watching the monks walk past in single file — and a slow boat day up the Mekong to the Pak Ou caves, with the thousand-Buddha grotto carved into the cliff. Plus a half-day at the Kuang Si waterfalls south of town (jungle, three turquoise tiers, swim at the lower one). And a long evening cooking class with chef Lao learning four classic Lao dishes including the famous larb of buffalo.

title: Coral reefs and pineapple farms of Japan's tropical south
shortDescription: 6 nights from Naha to Ishigaki and Taketomi with reef snorkels and a Ryukyu cooking class.
description:
Okinawa is the Japan most travellers don't know exists — subtropical, kind of Caribbean, with its own Ryukyuan language, its own food, and an unhurriedness you don't find on the main islands. The coral reefs are some of the best in Asia, and the longevity-research scientists keep coming back to figure out why the locals live forever.

Two nights in Naha, the Okinawa main island capital — Shuri castle, the covered Heiwa-dori market, a Ryukyu cooking class with a grandmother who teaches you goya champuru and sea-grape salad. A spirited evening at the Sakaemachi arcade for awamori, the local rice spirit.

Then a short flight south to the Yaeyama islands. Two nights on Ishigaki at a beach hotel with a kayak-out reef. A day to Taketomi by ferry — the smallest, prettiest of the islands, with red-tile roofs, white-sand paths, and water buffalo carts as the local taxi. Snorkel day at the manta point off Iriomote. Two nights back in a Naha boutique to finish. The slow pace of Okinawa is the whole point of going.

Seoul is the most over-caffeinated capital in Asia and also the most relaxing once you find the seams. title: Rainforest river, orangutans and the sea gypsies of Sabah
shortDescription: 7 nights through Sabah Borneo — Sepilok orangutans, Kinabatangan river lodge and the islands of Semporna.
description:
Borneo is what's left of the world before. The forest is older than the Amazon, the river runs brown and slow, and the orangutans you came to see really do still swing through the trees above your boat — but they're harder to find now than they were a generation ago, and watching the rehabilitation centres do their patient work is part of the trip.

Two nights in Sepilok, the orangutan rehabilitation centre on the east coast of Sabah, with a small jungle lodge five minutes' walk away. Morning feedings of the rehabilitated orangutans, the nursery for the orphans, and the next-door sun bear conservation centre. A night walk in the forest with a ranger.

Then two nights on the Kinabatangan river — a small eco-lodge on stilts above the water, dawn and dusk boats up and down the river to see proboscis monkeys, gibbons, hornbills, sometimes a wild orangutan in the trees, and at night the freshwater crocodiles' eyeshine on the surface. Then a long transfer south to Semporna for three nights of diving the islands of Mabul and Sipadan — one of the world's top five reefs, with the chance of hammerheads and barracuda walls.

title: Limestone lagoons and bangka days in the Bacuit archipelago
shortDescription: 7 nights between El Nido and Coron with island-hopping bangka days and a private cabana on the beach.
description:
Palawan keeps winning best-island-in-the-world polls and after a week there you stop being surprised. The Bacuit archipelago around El Nido is forty-five limestone islands rising vertically out of turquoise sea, with hidden lagoons inside some of them you can only enter by ducking under the cliff at low tide. The diving and snorkelling are why most people come, but the slow days on the beach are the real holiday.

Four nights in a small beach resort in El Nido, on a private bay reachable only by bangka — the traditional Filipino outrigger boat. Cabana on the sand, no road, breakfast on the deck. Two days of island-hopping by private bangka — the small lagoon, the big lagoon (only one boat at a time inside it), the secret beach with the tunnel entrance. A dusk swim at hidden beach.

Then three nights in Coron, four hours north by ferry — a quieter island with a string of Japanese WWII shipwrecks scattered around it for the wreck divers, freshwater Kayangan lake (the cleanest lake in Asia), and the Twin Lagoons connected by a passage under the cliff. The flight back to Manila on the last day passes over the islands and you'll be planning your return.

title: Cliff-edge monasteries in the Land of the Thunder Dragon
shortDescription: 7 nights through Bhutan — Paro, Thimphu, Punakha — with a Tiger's Nest hike and a homestay in Bumthang.
description:
Bhutan is the small Himalayan kingdom that measures itself in gross national happiness, charges a daily tourist fee to keep the volume low, and is impossible to do badly. The mountains are everywhere, every other building is a monastery, and the king is universally adored in a way that takes a while to get used to.

We build the trip around the four valleys. One night in Paro on arrival, then west to Thimphu (the world's only capital with no traffic lights), then over the Dochula pass to Punakha for the dzong (fortress monastery) on the river, then deeper east to Bumthang — the spiritual heart of the country, where Padmasambhava landed in the 8th century and which still feels like he might come back.

The famous one is the Tiger's Nest — the monastery clinging to a vertical cliff at 3000 metres, where you have to walk up a forest path for three hours to get there, and the building is somehow attached to the rock by what looks from below like nothing at all. We do this on day six when you're acclimatised. Bumthang is the slow heart of the trip — a farmhouse homestay with the family, archery in the field next door, butter tea, ema datshi (the chili-and-cheese national dish) and a hot-stone bath in a wooden tub.

title: A guided Annapurna circuit through Himalayan villages
shortDescription: 9 nights of guided trekking through the Annapurna foothills with a tea-house network and a porter team.
description:
The Annapurna circuit is one of the most beautiful trekking routes in the world without being one of the most technical. You walk an average of fifteen kilometres a day at altitudes between 1500 and 4000 metres, you sleep in tea houses run by Gurung and Thakali families, and the daily reward is a snow-mountain view from the dinner table.

We run the short, slow version — nine nights door to door, with one night in Kathmandu, one in Pokhara, and seven on the trail through the lower circuit (no high Thorong-La pass — that's for the longer trip). A licensed guide, a porter for each pair of trekkers, and the right pace for someone who's not been at altitude before.

The trekking itinerary is built around the views and the villages. Birethanti the first night, Ghorepani and the Poon Hill sunrise (the famous classic dawn over the Annapurna massif — Dhaulagiri 8167m, Annapurna South 7219m, Machapuchare 6993m), Tadapani, Chhomrong with the apple orchards, Jhinu Danda for the natural hot springs, and back to Pokhara via the village of Landruk. Comfortable lodges, hot showers most nights, dal bhat every evening that tastes better than anything in Nepal's capital.

title: Volcano cones, cloud-forest canopies and Pacific surf
shortDescription: 9 nights through Costa Rica — Arenal volcano, Monteverde cloud forest and a Manuel Antonio beach finale.
description:
Costa Rica gave up its army in 1949 and put the money into national parks. The result, three quarters of a century later, is that a country the size of West Virginia has more biodiversity per square kilometre than almost anywhere on earth — and an infrastructure for ecotourism that actually works.

We build the trip around three habitats. Three nights at Arenal — the famous cone-shaped volcano on the central plateau, with hot-spring rivers running through the rainforest, hanging bridges through the canopy, and a lodge with a balcony hot tub that has the volcano in it.

Then three nights in the Monteverde cloud forest — a cooler, wetter, higher world where the quetzals nest in the moss, the canopy zip lines launch you above the trees, and the night walks reveal eyelash vipers and red-eyed tree frogs that look like illustrations. Then three nights at Manuel Antonio on the Pacific coast — beach hotel above a long crescent of sand, the howler monkeys in the trees behind, surf lessons for beginners, sloths somewhere in every tree if you look hard enough.

title: Carioca beaches, Christ on the mountain and the great falls
shortDescription: 7 nights between Rio's Copacabana and an Iguazu lodge with helicopter view of the falls.
description:
Rio is the most beautifully placed major city in the world and one of the most argued-about. The mountains rise straight out of the ocean, the favelas climb up the hills behind, and the beach is the city's living room. Iguazu in the south is the wider, taller, louder of the two great South American waterfalls. Combined, it's the perfect introduction trip to Brazil.

Four nights in Rio in a small hotel above Copacabana, walking distance to the beach but on a quiet street. Mornings on the sand with the Sugarloaf in the distance and the surfers and the açaí vendors and the volleyball games already running by 8 am. Afternoons for the city — cable car up Sugarloaf at sunset, cog train up Corcovado for Christ the Redeemer when the haze burns off, an evening in Lapa for the samba and the caipirinhas.

Then three nights at a small lodge in the rainforest on the Brazilian side of Iguazu — the bigger half of the falls, with 275 separate cascades over almost three kilometres. The lodge has its own walking trail along the river to the famous Devil's Throat. A helicopter day for the aerial view. And a cross-border morning to the Argentine side, where the boardwalks take you above the falls themselves and the spray drenches you in a way you don't get from the Brazilian distance.

title: Tango nights and the blue ice of the Perito Moreno
shortDescription: 9 nights between Buenos Aires and Patagonia with a tango night and the Perito Moreno glacier.
description:
Argentina is two countries — the Italian-French Buenos Aires of the wine bars and the wide avenues, and the Patagonian south of the windswept plains, glaciers and condors. Nine nights gives you both.

Four nights in Buenos Aires in a Palermo boutique. Mornings of long coffees in Recoleta cafés, afternoons at the MALBA museum and the Recoleta cemetery (where Evita is buried in the middle of one of the most absurd cities of the dead anywhere). Evenings in San Telmo for tango — a proper milonga with locals dancing rather than a tourist show. A long Sunday lunch of asado at a Palermo parrilla.

Then five nights in Patagonia. Two nights in El Calafate for the Perito Moreno glacier — one of the few advancing glaciers left on earth, with house-sized icebergs calving into the lake every twenty minutes. A boat day on the lake among the icebergs and an ice-walk on the glacier itself with crampons. Then three nights at El Chaltén in the Fitz Roy massif for the trekking trails to Laguna de los Tres, the granite spires that gave Patagonia clothing its logo. Last morning back to Calafate and the long flight home.

title: Mayan ruins, cenote swims and a Tulum beach finale
shortDescription: 8 nights through Yucatán — Mérida colonial, Chichén Itzá, cenotes and a Tulum jungle hotel.
description:
The Yucatán is one of those rare places where every cliché is real. The cenotes (limestone sinkholes filled with crystal-clear groundwater) are exactly as turquoise as the photos. Chichén Itzá at dawn is exactly as awe-inspiring as it sounds. The Tulum beach hotels that look like they're built out of palm leaves and hammocks really are. And the food everywhere is staggeringly good.

Three nights in Mérida — the colonial capital, with mariachi in the Plaza Grande on Saturday and the henequen-baron mansions on the Paseo de Montejo. A small heritage hotel in the centre, breakfast in a courtyard, afternoon at the Anthropology museum with the best Maya collection outside Mexico City.

Then two nights at a hacienda hotel near Chichén Itzá — pre-dawn private entry to see the temple of Kukulkán before the buses come, then a day of cenote swimming. Then three nights in Tulum — a thatched-roof beach hotel on the strip, no electricity in the rooms after 11 pm, the walls of the ancient Maya port-city of Tulum two minutes' walk away. A boat morning at Sian Ka'an biosphere reserve with the dolphins and a long lazy beach finish.

title: Old Havana, vintage cars and the tobacco valleys
shortDescription: 7 nights between Havana, Viñales tobacco valley and a Trinidad colonial townhouse.
description:
Cuba is a slow trip in a fast country. The cars are still 1950s, the buildings are still 1920s, the internet barely works, and the music starts at 11 in the morning and continues until everyone needs to sleep. A week is the right length to see the three places that matter.

Three nights in Havana in a casa particular — a Cuban-family-run B&B in a converted colonial townhouse in Habana Vieja, two minutes from the cathedral square. Mornings of walks through the old town with a historian, afternoons of the Museum of the Revolution and a vintage-car ride along the Malecón. Evenings at La Bodeguita del Medio (where Hemingway drank his mojitos) and a late jazz set at La Zorra y el Cuervo.

Then two nights in Viñales — the tobacco country two hours west, where the limestone karsts called mogotes rise out of the red fields. A homestay with a tobacco-farming family, a visit to a cigar-rolling workshop, a horseback ride through the valley. Then two nights in Trinidad, the perfectly preserved 18th-century sugar town in the south — cobbled streets, pastel townhouses, salsa in the Casa de la Música at midnight, and an afternoon at Playa Ancón on the Caribbean for a swim.

title: Blue-footed boobies, marine iguanas and a Darwin yacht
shortDescription: 7 nights on a small naturalist-guided yacht through the Galápagos islands with daily snorkels and walks.
description:
The Galápagos are the closest a regular trip gets to feeling like a science expedition. The wildlife doesn't know to be afraid of people — the boobies dance their courtship in front of you, the sea lions swim around your snorkel mask, the giant tortoises just keep eating. Charles Darwin spent five weeks here and changed science. You get a week and change yourself.

The right way to do the Galápagos is by yacht rather than land-based. We put you on a small expedition yacht — 16 cabins, naturalist guide, dinghy fleet, sails between islands at night so every morning you wake up somewhere different. The yacht is private to its 32 guests, with the same naturalist with you all week.

The itinerary covers the central and northern islands — Santa Cruz with the Charles Darwin research station and the giant tortoise reserve, Genovesa for the red-footed boobies and frigatebirds, Bartolomé for the panoramic Pinnacle Rock view and the snorkel with Galápagos penguins (the only penguins on the equator), Isabela for the volcano walks, Floreana for the Post Office Bay tradition. Two nights bookended in Quito at the start and the end for the high-altitude colonial old town.

shortDescription: 7 nights between Banff and Lake Louise with the Icefields Parkway and a helicopter glacier landing.

The Canadian Rockies are the ridiculously photogenic part of the country, and the photogenic-ness of the lakes is real — the rock flour from the glaciers gives the water that impossible turquoise colour you've seen on every desktop background.

Three nights in Banff, the small mountain town inside the national park, in a heritage hotel with a hot spring at the foot of Sulphur Mountain. Mornings on the Banff gondola, afternoons at the Cave and Basin hot springs, evenings on the Bow river boardwalk with elk grazing in the meadows on the way back.

A wildlife morning with a bear-aware ranger for grizzly, black bear and possibly wolf. And a slow last day at the spa.

title: From the Golden Gate down Highway 1 to Big Sur
shortDescription: 9 nights driving from San Francisco to Los Angeles via Monterey, Big Sur and Santa Barbara.
description:
Highway 1 down the California coast is one of those drives that justifies itself entirely on the scenery. Nine hundred kilometres of road on the cliff edge above the Pacific, sea otters and elephant seals on the beaches below, redwoods on the inland side, and an unreasonable concentration of good restaurants along the way.

Two nights in San Francisco in a small Nob Hill hotel — cable cars at the door, the bridge in the distance, walking distance to Chinatown and North Beach. A morning at Alcatraz, an afternoon at Golden Gate park, evening dinner at Tartine.

Then down the coast slowly. Two nights in Monterey for Big Sur — the famous stretch where the road actually carves into the cliff and the wide turnouts give you a hundred ways to look at the Pacific. Sunset on Bixby Bridge, a long lunch at Nepenthe perched above the sea. Then two nights in Santa Barbara for the Spanish colonial old town and a long wine afternoon in the hills. Then three nights in Los Angeles — a Venice Beach hotel, a long brunch at Gjelina, a Griffith Observatory sunset, and the Getty Museum on the last morning before the long flight home.

title: Aztec temples, mezcal nights and a Day-of-the-Dead Oaxaca
shortDescription: 7 nights between Mexico City's Roma Norte and Oaxaca with a Frida day and a mezcal palenque morning.
description:
Mexico City is the most underrated capital in the Americas — Aztec ruins inside the modern centre, a museum collection that beats most of Europe's, the highest concentration of small-batch mezcal bars on earth, and a food scene that goes from $2 al pastor tacos to two-Michelin-star tasting menus, often on the same block.

Four nights in a small boutique in Roma Norte, the leafy neighbourhood between Condesa and the historical centre. Mornings of the museums — the Anthropology museum (one of the great ones), the Frida Kahlo blue house in Coyoacán. Afternoons of the old centre — the Templo Mayor Aztec ruins, the Diego Rivera murals in the Palacio Nacional. Evenings at Pujol or Contramar for the food, or a mezcal bar in La Roma for the cheaper, better version.

Then three nights in Oaxaca — the southern colonial city that's the spiritual heart of mezcal, mole and the Day of the Dead. A heritage hotel near the Zócalo. A long morning at the Monte Albán ruins above the valley, a mezcal palenque visit out in the agave fields to see how the spirit is actually made (cooked in earth ovens, crushed by a horse-pulled stone wheel), and an evening market crawl through the seven famous mole sauces. If you can be there for Día de los Muertos in early November, do.

title: Mars-like desert, salt flats and the world's clearest sky
shortDescription: 6 nights at a small Atacama lodge with stargazing, the Tatio geysers and the salt flats of Atacama.
description:
The Atacama is the driest desert on earth — there are weather stations that haven't recorded rain in decades — which has two consequences. The first is that the landscape looks like Mars. The second is that the sky has zero humidity and the world's clearest view of the stars, which is why ALMA, the world's largest radio observatory, is on a plateau an hour up the road.

We put you in a small lodge in San Pedro de Atacama, the adobe village at 2400m altitude that's the base for everything. Adobe walls, a courtyard with a fire pit, a small pool. Acclimatisation is gentle — the first day is slow, sunset at Moon Valley, and you stay around the village until day three.

Then the excursions ramp up. The Tatio geysers at dawn at 4300m — eighty geysers steaming in the cold morning, hot springs to swim in afterwards. The Atacama salt flat with the flamingos in the brine ponds and the Andes behind. A night with an astronomer at a private observatory above the village, where the milky way is bright enough to cast shadows. And a slow last day at Termas de Puritama, the natural hot-spring terraced pools in a desert canyon.

title: Walled cities, coffee farms and a Rosario island day
shortDescription: 7 nights between Cartagena's walled old town and a coffee-finca stay in the Zona Cafetera.
description:
Colombia rewards the traveller who came twenty years late to the party — the cities are safe, the coffee is the best in the world, and the colonial Caribbean towns like Cartagena are some of the most photogenic in the Americas. We give you the Caribbean side and the coffee country in one week.

Four nights in Cartagena in a converted 17th-century mansion inside the walled city — three storeys, an interior courtyard with a fountain, a roof terrace with a small plunge pool and a view of the colourful bougainvillea facades next door. Mornings of slow walks through the old town with a local guide. Afternoons in Getsemaní — the rougher, cooler neighbourhood next door where the street art is great and the salsa starts early.

A day on the Rosario islands — a small boat through the Caribbean, an empty beach lunch, a swim in the bioluminescent lagoon at night. Then three nights at a coffee finca in the Zona Cafetera near Salento. Sleeping in a hacienda built in the 1890s, walking through the coffee bushes with the picker family, learning to roast and cup like a barista, and a slow Sunday in the Cocora valley where the wax palms grow to 60 metres.

title: Geysers, bison herds and the spires of the Grand Tetons
shortDescription: 7 nights between a Jackson Hole lodge and inside Yellowstone with a private wildlife guide.
description:
Yellowstone is the world's first national park (1872) and still its most extraordinary. Half a continent's worth of geothermal activity stuffed into one caldera — 500 geysers, thousands of hot springs, the largest concentration of free-ranging megafauna in the lower 48 — and right next to it the granite spires of the Grand Tetons, the most beautifully sudden mountains in North America.

We split your week. Three nights at a lodge in Jackson Hole at the foot of the Tetons — wood-and-stone cabin, fireplace, a deck looking at the peaks. Mornings on the Snake River by raft, afternoons in the cottonwood meadows where the moose graze. A long sunset at Schwabacher Landing with the Tetons reflected.

Then four nights inside Yellowstone at the Old Faithful Inn (the historic log-built lodge inside the park) and Lake Yellowstone Hotel. A private wildlife guide for two days — Lamar Valley at dawn for the wolf packs and the bison herds, Hayden Valley for the grizzlies. Old Faithful itself, the Grand Prismatic spring from above, the Norris geyser basin, the Yellowstone Grand Canyon falls. And one slow morning at the lake watching the elk swim across at first light.

title: French Quarter mornings, swamp afternoons and a brass-band night
shortDescription: 5 nights in a French Quarter townhouse with a swamp tour, a jazz crawl and a po'boy walking tour.
description:
New Orleans is the most foreign city in the United States and the most southern city in the United States, and the food and the music both follow from that. The brass bands play in the street, the gumbo is properly Creole, and the cemeteries are above ground because the city is below sea level.

Five nights in a converted Creole townhouse in the French Quarter, on a balcony street two blocks from Bourbon but quiet enough to actually sleep. Mornings of beignets at Café du Monde and a long walk through Jackson Square. Afternoons at the National WWII Museum (one of the best in the country) or a streetcar ride down St Charles Avenue past the antebellum mansions.

The nights are about the music. A jazz set at Preservation Hall in the Quarter, a second-line parade through the Marigny if you're lucky, a late set at Snug Harbor in Frenchmen Street, and a brass-band brunch at Buffa's. The day-trip is a swamp tour by airboat through the bayous south of the city — alligators, herons, cypress knees, Spanish moss. And a po'boy walking tour through Treme and the Lower Garden District to taste five sandwiches at five small joints.

title: Pyramids, pharaonic temples and a slow Nile dahabiya
shortDescription: 9 nights between Cairo and a dahabiya cruise up the Nile from Luxor to Aswan with private temple access.
description:
Egypt has been a destination since Herodotus wrote about it in 450 BC and it still works for the same reasons — the pyramids are still there, the Nile still flows north, and the temples of Karnak and Abu Simbel still produce that physical jolt of standing in front of something so old it doesn't really belong to time anymore.

Three nights in Cairo in a heritage hotel in Garden City — the old diplomatic neighbourhood, a short drive from the museum and across the river from Giza. The new Grand Egyptian Museum opening 2024 with all of Tutankhamun's grave goods together for the first time. A private dawn visit to the pyramids and the Sphinx before the bus crowds.

Then the cruise. Five nights on a small dahabiya — a traditional twin-sail wooden Nile boat with eight cabins, sailing up from Luxor to Aswan slowly, anchoring at temples the big cruise ships can't reach. Karnak, Edfu, Kom Ombo, Philae. Private temple access in the evenings when the day groups leave. One night at Abu Simbel — the colossal Ramses statues that were moved up the cliff in the 1960s to escape the lake. Last night back in Cairo for the souks of Khan El Khalili.

title: Big-five plains and a Masai village in the great migration
shortDescription: 7 nights between a Nairobi heritage hotel and a luxury Mara safari camp during the great migration season.
description:
The Masai Mara during the great migration is the most concentrated wildlife spectacle on earth. Two million wildebeest, zebra and gazelle move north from the Serengeti, cross the crocodile-filled Mara river, and the predators that follow them turn the whole ecosystem into a kind of nature-documentary you stop being able to believe is real.

We build your trip around four nights at a luxury tented camp on the edge of the Mara reserve. Big canvas tents with hardwood floors, hot showers, private deck, dawn coffee delivered by the Masai staff. Morning and evening game drives in a 4x4 with a Kenyan naturalist guide who's been doing this for twenty years. A river-crossing morning if the migration timing aligns. A Masai village afternoon. A balloon ride over the plains at dawn.

We bookend the trip with two nights in Nairobi at a heritage hotel — a slow first day to acclimatise, the Giraffe Centre and the Karen Blixen house, dinner at the carnivore restaurant. And one last night at the camp before the long flight home. Wildlife sightings are never guaranteed but in this camp the big-five list usually gets ticked off in the first 48 hours.

title: Crater walls, Serengeti lions and a Zanzibar beach finale
shortDescription: 10 nights from the Ngorongoro crater through the Serengeti to a Zanzibar beach finale.
description:
Tanzania does the safari at scale and the beach at scale and combines them better than anywhere on the continent. Ten nights gives you both the wildlife of the Ngorongoro crater and the Serengeti and a proper week of recovery on the white-sand beaches of Zanzibar.

One night in Arusha to start. Two nights at a lodge on the rim of the Ngorongoro crater — a 600-metre drop straight down into a perfect circle of grassland with the densest population of mammals on earth. Dawn game drives down on the floor with rhinos, lions, hippo pools and the black-maned lions of the crater.

Then three nights in the Serengeti at a moving camp that follows the migration. Big canvas tents, dawn drives, a sundowner under an acacia tree. Wildebeest plains in numbers no other ecosystem produces. Then four nights in Zanzibar at a beach resort on the north-east coast — a thatched-roof villa twenty steps from the sand, snorkel from the dock, spice-tour morning in the inland gardens, a sunset dhow cruise. A Stone Town walking afternoon for the carved Arab doors and the slave-trade history.

title: Red dunes, desert-adapted elephants and the Skeleton Coast
shortDescription: 8 nights driving Namibia — Sossusvlei dunes, Damaraland, Etosha pan and a Skeleton Coast morning.
description:
Namibia is the most empty country on earth that's safe to drive yourself. Twice the size of Germany with two and a half million people, fewer roads than Belgium, dunes the height of the Eiffel tower, and a skeleton coast where the shipwrecks lie next to elephant footprints.

We build the trip around three landscapes. Two nights at Sossusvlei — the dunes you've seen on every Namibia poster, the orange sand against the bleached camel-thorn trees of Deadvlei, the climb up Big Daddy (the world's tallest dune at 325m). A self-drive lodge with a small pool and a deck looking at the desert.

Then two nights in Damaraland — the rocky desert north, where the desert-adapted elephants survive on what no other elephants will eat, and the ancient San rock engravings at Twyfelfontein are 6000 years old. A small camp with canvas tents on stilts. Three nights at Etosha — the great salt pan and game park of the north, with elephant, giraffe, lion at the waterholes. One night at the Skeleton Coast — a remote lodge with the Atlantic at the door, seal colonies, shipwrecks half-buried in the sand. Last night back in Windhoek.

title: Mokoros, lion roars and a flooded Kalahari
shortDescription: 7 nights through Botswana — Okavango delta, Moremi reserve and the Linyanti — by mokoro, 4x4 and walking.
description:
The Okavango delta is the most extraordinary wetland on earth — a river that flows into the desert and never reaches the sea, and on the way creates 18000 square kilometres of seasonal flooded papyrus and palm islands that fill with elephant, hippo, lion and one of the densest leopard populations anywhere. Botswana's high-cost-low-impact tourism model means there are about four other vehicles in the whole delta and the rest is yours.

We put you in three small luxury camps over the week. Two nights at a water camp inside the delta — eight tents, no roads, you arrive by light aircraft, all transfers from the camp are by mokoro (the traditional poled dugout canoe) through reed channels above the hippos. Then two nights at a Moremi land-and-water camp on the eastern side for big-game drives in the 4x4. Then three nights at a Linyanti camp on the river border with Namibia for elephant herds at the river and night drives for leopards.

Every day starts with a 5:30 am coffee at the deck. Every evening ends with a sundowner under an ebony tree. Lion roars at 3 am. Hippo grunts at all times. It is one of the great trips on earth and you will not stop dreaming about it.

title: Mountain gorillas in the Volcanoes National Park
shortDescription: 5 nights between a Kigali design hotel and a Volcanoes lodge with two gorilla trekking permits.
description:
There are roughly a thousand mountain gorillas left on earth and they all live in the high cloud forest where Rwanda, Uganda and the DRC meet. The Volcanoes National Park on the Rwandan side has been running gorilla trekking carefully since the 1980s — eight people per family per day, one hour with the gorillas, $1500 per permit, and the money keeps the gorillas alive.

Five nights split between Kigali and the volcanoes. Two nights in Kigali in a design hotel in the leafy Kiyovu neighbourhood. The slow first day is the genocide memorial — heavy but the essential context for everything that follows in Rwanda. Coffee at Question Coffee, a long lunch at Fusion, an evening walk through Nyamirambo to see the city by night.

Then three nights at a lodge on the edge of the Volcanoes National Park — wooden cottages with fireplaces, hot showers, a hot water bottle in the bed because at 2500m it gets cold at night. Two gorilla treks (we book two permits because every family is different and the second trek often beats the first). A half-day to the Bisate village to see the conservation work the lodges do for the surrounding communities. And a long evening with a bottle of red watching the volcanoes change colour at sunset.

title: Lemurs in the rainforest and the avenue of baobabs
shortDescription: 9 nights across Madagascar — Andasibe lemurs, the avenue of baobabs and a Nosy Be beach finale.
description:
Madagascar is the fourth-largest island in the world and roughly 90 percent of what lives on it lives only there. Six species of baobab grow nowhere else. A hundred and ten species of lemur, all endemic. The flora is so weird that botanists call the spiny forest of the south its own ecosystem.

Nine nights gives you three habitats. Two nights in Antananarivo at the start in a colonial hill hotel — the markets, the queen's palace, a slow first day to acclimatise to driving on dirt roads. Then two nights at Andasibe-Mantadia national park, the most accessible rainforest in the east — indri lemurs (the loudest land animal on earth, calling at dawn from the trees behind the lodge), night walks for mouse lemurs and chameleons.

Then the famous one. A short flight west to Morondava and two nights at a beach hotel near the Avenue of the Baobabs — the line of 30-metre baobabs that's the most photographed road in Madagascar, especially at sunset when the locals walk between the trees with their cattle. A day trip south to Kirindy reserve for the fossa, the cat-like top predator. Finally three nights at Nosy Be in the north for the beach — turquoise water, snorkel from the dock, last sundowner on the sand.

title: Granite-boulder beaches and giant tortoises
shortDescription: 7 nights island-hopping Mahé, Praslin and La Digue with a granite-boulder beach and a giant-tortoise reserve.
description:
The Seychelles is the kind of beach that ruined other beaches. Granite boulders the size of houses scattered along stretches of white sand, the most photogenic coconut palms in the Indian Ocean, and a population so small that you can still find a beach with no one else on it on a Tuesday morning. The three main islands give you a different version of the same paradise.

Three nights on Mahé, the main island, at a resort tucked into a quiet north-coast bay. Walking distance to Beau Vallon for the snorkel, a hike up Morne Blanc, a long lunch at Marie-Antoinette's Creole restaurant in Victoria. A day on the Praslin ferry to see the Vallée de Mai — the prehistoric palm forest where the famous coco de mer grows, the world's largest nut and the most suggestively shaped one too.

Then two nights on Praslin at a beach hotel on Anse Lazio — voted best beach in the world more often than is plausible. Then two nights on La Digue, the small island next door, reached by ferry — the iconic Anse Source d'Argent with the granite boulders, bicycles as the only transport, the giant Aldabra tortoises in the L'Union Estate reserve. Last sunset back on Mahé.

title: Reef lagoons, Creole curries and the gorges of the south
shortDescription: 7 nights at a Mauritius beach resort with a south-island Black River Gorges hike and an Île aux Cerfs day.
description:
Mauritius is the more accessible alternative to its more famous Indian Ocean neighbours — a French-Creole-Indian-Chinese mix of cultures, the best curries between Mumbai and Cape Town, a lagoon all the way around the island where you can wade out half a kilometre and the water never goes above your waist.

We put you at a small beach resort on the quieter north-east coast, on a bay protected by the outer reef. Thatched-roof villa twenty metres from the lagoon, breakfast on the deck, a small infinity pool, daily massage included. Most of the week is the slow beach week — snorkel from the dock, paddleboard across the lagoon at dawn, a kite-surf lesson if you want.

The two big day-trips are inland and offshore. A day in the Black River Gorges — the green volcanic interior of the south with the 800-metre waterfalls and the seven coloured earths of Chamarel — and a long lunch at the rum distillery there. And a private boat day to Île aux Cerfs on the east coast — a small offshore island with white sand and turquoise lagoon. Plus a half-day in Port Louis market for the proper Creole street food. Last sunset on the deck with the lagoon glassy.

title: Tanneries, blue alleys and a slow road to the Sahara
shortDescription: 9 nights through Morocco's imperial cities — Fez, Chefchaouen, Meknès and Volubilis — to a Sahara camp.
description:
Morocco beyond Marrakech is a different and slower country. The imperial cities of the north — Fez, Meknès, Volubilis — are older, less polished and more rewarding. The blue town of Chefchaouen in the Rif mountains is genuinely as blue as the photos. And the dunes of Erg Chebbi at the edge of the Sahara are the postcard version of a desert at scale.

Three nights in Fez in a riad in the medieval medina — the oldest unchanged urban quarter in the world, a UNESCO site that still functions as a working city. Mornings of tanneries (smell-strong but visually astonishing) and the Al-Qarawiyyin university (founded 859, world's oldest), afternoons of the souks with a local guide who knows the routes that don't go past the tour groups. A long evening on the riad roof with the call to prayer from the surrounding mosques.

Then two nights in Chefchaouen — a town painted entirely in blue, with mountain streams running through the centre, in a guesthouse on a quiet alley. Then one night at Volubilis (the Roman ruins) and Meknès (the imperial city). Then the long drive south across the Atlas to Merzouga and two nights at a Sahara camp — Berber tents at the foot of the dunes, sunset camel ride into the sand, dinner by firelight, a sky like you don't get in Europe. Last night back in Fez before flying home.
