title: Fiords, glaciers and a Queenstown road trip
shortDescription: 9 nights driving NZ's South Island — Christchurch, Aoraki, Wanaka, Queenstown and a Milford Sound day.
description:
The South Island of New Zealand is the most concentrated landscape country on earth — the Southern Alps run almost the whole length of it, the fiords are deeper than the mountains are tall, and most of the population lives in two towns. Self-drive is the only proper way to see it.

One night in Christchurch on arrival, then up to Aoraki/Mt Cook for two nights — the highest peak in the country, the alpine villages, the Tasman glacier boat that takes you among the icebergs. Then over the Lindis pass to Wanaka for two nights — the lake town with the famous tree growing out of the water, a slow hike to Roy's Peak (1500m of climb, the postcard view at the top). Then on to Queenstown for three nights — the adventure capital, gondola up the Ben Lomond, an evening at Amisfield winery.

The big day is Milford Sound — a long drive through the Eglinton valley with the snow-fed waterfalls beside the road, then a small-boat cruise into the fiord with the Mitre Peak rising 1700m straight out of the water. We add a helicopter day from Queenstown over the Glaciers and Fiordland if the weather opens up. Last night back in Christchurch for the flight home.

title: Volcanoes, geothermal pools and a Maori hangi night
shortDescription: 7 nights through NZ's North Island — Auckland, Hobbiton, Rotorua geothermal and the Bay of Islands.
description:
The North Island is the warmer, friendlier, more Polynesian half of New Zealand — geothermal valleys hissing steam, Maori marae (meeting houses) where you're welcomed properly in the traditional way, and a 144-island bay at the very top with dolphins and a hole in the rock you can drive a boat through.

Two nights in Auckland in a small Ponsonby boutique. A morning at the Maritime Museum, a walk up Mount Eden volcano for the view, a long lunch on the harbour. A day trip south to Hobbiton — the still-standing Lord of the Rings set in the rolling hills near Matamata, surreal and very photographed.

Then three nights in Rotorua — the geothermal town in the centre of the island, where mud pools bubble in the public park and the sulphur smell is part of the air. A traditional Maori hangi dinner at the marae (food cooked in a steam pit dug in the ground), a morning at Wai-O-Tapu's geyser and silica terraces, an evening at the Polynesian Spa hot pools above the lake. Then two nights at the Bay of Islands at the top of the country — a small lodge above the harbour at Russell, a sailing day to the hole in the rock, a swim with dolphins (responsibly, with a licensed boat).

title: Coral atolls, reef snorkels and a Yasawa island week
shortDescription: 7 nights at a Yasawa islands resort with a private bure, daily snorkels and a manta-ray day.
description:
Fiji is one of those places where you don't really need much beyond a beach, a snorkel mask and a hammock. The Yasawa islands on the west of the country are the version of the Pacific that doesn't exist in postcards because the postcards somehow don't quite catch it.

We put you on a small adults-only resort on one of the Yasawa islands, reached by a 90-minute catamaran from Nadi. A private bure (the traditional thatched Fijian villa) right on a small white-sand beach, with a hammock between two palm trees and a snorkel-from-the-deck reef in front. Eight bures total on the whole resort.

The daytime is whatever you want. The reef is healthy and the visibility is the famously good Pacific kind. There's a small kayak available, a sunset paddleboard option, a sea-kayak day to a tiny uninhabited islet off the next bay. A morning boat north to the Sawa-i-Lau caves — limestone sea caves that the Fijian boys jump into from the cliff at low tide. A manta-ray boat day in the right season (May-October). And one cultural afternoon at the Fijian village two coves north — kava ceremony with the chief, a meke (traditional dance) at sunset, walk with the schoolchildren.

Glass floor with stingrays passing under at sunset, private deck with a plunge pool, direct ladder access to the lagoon, breakfast brought to the deck by canoe. A lagoon tour with snorkel stops at the coral garden and the shark-and-ray pool (lemon and blacktip reef sharks come to the boat in waist-deep water and they are not interested in you). A guided 4x4 morning around the main island. A sunset cruise around Mount Otemanu. The rest is the hammock.

shortDescription: 7 nights between Cairns, the Daintree rainforest and a Lizard Island reef resort with daily reef days.
description:
The Great Barrier Reef is the largest living structure on earth and you can see it from space. It is also slowly dying, and the right thing to do is to see it now with a guide who can explain what's happening and how the reef-protection efforts are working. Tropical north Queensland combines the reef with the world's oldest rainforest a few kilometres inland.

Two nights in Cairns to start at a small boutique near the Esplanade. A morning at the Botanic Gardens, a sunset on the Cairns boardwalk, dinner at Ochre. A long day on the reef from Cairns — a high-end small-boat day with a reef biologist, two snorkel sites at the outer reef, lunch on board.

Then two nights in the Daintree — the 130-million-year-old rainforest north of Cairns where the cassowaries and the saltwater crocodiles live, with the Mossman Gorge for the morning swim. A canopy walk and a night-light spotlight tour for the bandicoots and the tree-frogs. Then three nights at Lizard Island — a small luxury resort on a national-park island 250 km north of Cairns, reached by light aircraft. Snorkel from the dock onto the giant clam garden, sea-kayak to an empty beach, and the famous Cod Hole reef dive ten minutes from shore.

title: The big red rock and an aboriginal dot-painting class
shortDescription: 5 nights at an Uluru desert lodge with sunset on the rock, Field of Light and a Kata Tjuta walk.
description:
Uluru is the spiritual heart of Australia and one of those rare geological features that look as monumental in person as the postcards have made them seem. The colour really does change through the day. The 9-kilometre walk around the base really does take you into a different world. The Anangu people whose land it is have been here for 30,000 years and the proper way to see it is with their guides telling their stories.

Five nights at a small desert lodge a short drive from the rock. Tented rooms with hardwood floors and outdoor showers, a central campfire, a swimming pool that feels surreal in the red dust. Mornings of base walks with an Anangu guide for the rock-art sites and the waterhole at Mutitjulu, afternoons in the visitor centre learning the Tjukurpa creation stories.

Three experiences you don't miss. The sunset on the rock from the special viewing area as the colour goes through the whole spectrum from ochre to red to purple to black. The Field of Light installation — 50,000 solar lights covering the desert below the rock in a slow colour change after dark. And a guided walk through Kata Tjuta (the older, taller, less famous rock formation 50 km west) with a Maori-Anangu guide for the Valley of the Winds. A dot-painting workshop with a local artist on the last morning.

title: Rose-red Petra and a Bedouin camp under the desert stars
shortDescription: 6 nights through Jordan — Amman, Dead Sea, Petra and a Wadi Rum Bedouin camp.
description:
Jordan is one of those countries that packs three world-class experiences into a country the size of Hungary. The Roman ruins, the rose-red city of Petra carved into a desert canyon, and the lunar landscape of Wadi Rum where Lawrence of Arabia and The Martian were filmed. Six nights does all three properly.

One night in Amman to acclimatise — a small hotel in Jabal Amman, the old colonial neighbourhood, with a long lunch at Sufra and a sunset at the Citadel above the city. Then two nights at a Dead Sea resort — the lowest point on earth at 430m below sea level, where the salinity is so high you literally cannot sink and the mineral mud on the shore is what the Cleopatra-marketed spa products are made from.

Then two nights in Petra. A hotel by the visitor centre, three minutes' walk to the Siq — the kilometre-long natural slot canyon that opens onto the Treasury facade at the end. A full day at the site, a Petra-by-Night candle evening, and a second day to climb the 800 steps to the Monastery at the back of the site. Then one night in Wadi Rum at a Bedouin-style camp — 4x4 morning through the dunes and the rock arches, sunset on a high cliff, dinner under more stars than you can hold in your head, sleep in a tent with a glass dome looking up at the milky way.

title: Three faiths in one old city and a Masada dawn
shortDescription: 6 nights between Jerusalem's old city, Tel Aviv beaches and a Masada-Dead Sea desert day.
description:
Jerusalem is one of the few cities on earth where you can walk between three of the world's great religious sites in twenty minutes — the Western Wall, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the Dome of the Rock. It is dense, intense, often overwhelming, and the only way to do it is with a great guide and enough time to recover between the heavy bits.

Three nights in Jerusalem in a small heritage hotel in the German colony — quiet residential streets, walking distance to the old city through Yemin Moshe and the Mamilla promenade. Mornings in the old city with a guide who knows the four quarters (Christian, Muslim, Jewish, Armenian) and the protocol at each holy site. Afternoons at Yad Vashem (the holocaust museum, heavy and essential), the Israel Museum (for the Dead Sea Scrolls), and the Mahane Yehuda market for the food.

A dawn on the Masada plateau — Roman siege ramp, 2000-year-old palace, the sunrise over the Dead Sea below. A long Dead Sea float afterwards. Then three nights in Tel Aviv at a small hotel near Neve Tzedek. Mornings on the beach with the spaniels and the coffee, afternoons in the Bauhaus white-city neighbourhood, evenings at the Carmel market and the small jazz bars of Florentin. A long lunch in Jaffa overlooking the Mediterranean.

title: Wadis, frankincense forts and the dunes of the Empty Quarter
shortDescription: 8 nights through Oman — Muscat, the Hajar mountains, Nizwa fort and a Wahiba Sands camp.
description:
Oman is the Gulf state that didn't lose its mind during the oil boom. Sultan Qaboos spent the petrodollars on heritage preservation instead of skyscrapers, and the result is a country where the forts are real, the souks still smell of frankincense, and the dunes of the Empty Quarter look exactly like they did when Wilfred Thesiger crossed them in 1948.

Two nights in Muscat in a coastal boutique. Morning at the Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque (one of the most beautiful modern mosques on earth, with the world's second-largest hand-woven carpet), afternoon at the Mutrah souk for the frankincense and silver.

Then three nights at a mountain lodge in the Hajar at 2000m — cooler air, terraced villages, walks along the falaj (irrigation channels) of the Saiq Plateau, the abandoned village of Wadi Bani Habib hanging on a cliff. A long lunch at Nizwa fort with the Friday goat market. Two nights at the edge of the Wahiba Sands — Bedouin-style camp at the foot of the dunes, sunset camel ride, sand-boarding for the energetic, dinner under the stars. Last night back in Muscat at the coast.

title: Hot-air balloons over fairy chimneys and a cave-hotel night
shortDescription: 5 nights in a Cappadocia cave hotel with a sunrise balloon ride, underground cities and a horseback day.
description:
Cappadocia is the surreal volcanic plateau in central Turkey where wind and rain have carved the soft tuff rock into honeycomb cliffs, fairy chimneys and underground cities. The Hittites, the early Christians and the Cappadocians themselves have all carved cities into the rock here, and you can still sleep in one. The hot-air balloons at dawn are the postcard image and they are real.

Five nights in a cave hotel in Göreme — actual carved-into-the-rock bedrooms, vaulted stone ceilings, a courtyard with a fireplace, breakfast on a terrace looking at the fairy chimneys. Mornings of fairy-chimney walks through the Love Valley and the Rose Valley, afternoons at the Göreme open-air museum (Byzantine cave churches with frescoes from the 10th century).

A balloon ride at dawn — 4 am wake, 90-minute flight over the chimneys as the sun comes up, champagne breakfast on landing. A day at the underground city of Derinkuyu — eight storeys down, where 20,000 people hid from raiders in the Byzantine period. A horseback morning through the valleys (Cappadocia literally means 'land of the beautiful horses' in old Persian). And a sunset at the Red Valley viewpoint, which is the second-most photographed view in Turkey.

title: Hagia Sophia, the Grand Bazaar and a Bosphorus evening
shortDescription: 4 nights in a Sultanahmet boutique with private Topkapı, Grand Bazaar and a sunset Bosphorus cruise.
description:
Istanbul is the only city in the world that straddles two continents, and every emperor from Constantine to Süleyman tried to make it the centre of the universe. The result is a layered city of Byzantine churches turned mosques, palace gardens, and the kind of bazaar that's been there for 600 years and still works the same way.

Four nights in a small Ottoman-house boutique in Sultanahmet, the old peninsula — walking distance to Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque and Topkapı, on a quiet alley below the Hippodrome. Mornings at the monuments with a historian, afternoons at the Basilica Cistern and the new Istanbul Modern across the Golden Horn.

The two famous mornings. A guided early-entry visit to Topkapı for the harem and the treasury. The Grand Bazaar with a local who knows which han to look in for the actual antiques (and which carpet dealer not to bother with). A Spice Bazaar walk with tea and çiğ köfte. A sunset cruise on the Bosphorus with the muezzin's call to prayer floating over the water from a half-dozen minarets. And a slow last morning across at the Asian-side Kadıköy fish market for the proper meze. A hammam afternoon at one of the historical baths.
